---
title: "Ensemble Methods"
---

Ensembles combine many weak or unstable learners to improve predictive
performance. This lecture focuses on bagging, random forests, boosting,
and the statistical idea of variance reduction.

## Learning Objectives

- Explain why averaging reduces variance.
- Compare bagging and random forests.
- Describe boosting as sequential error-focused learning.
- Tune ensemble models without leaking test information.

## Core Ideas

Bagging builds many models on bootstrap samples and averages their
predictions. Random forests decorrelate the trees by sampling predictors
at each split. Boosting builds models sequentially so later learners
focus on patterns missed by earlier ones.

## Bagging

Bagging reduces variance by averaging many trees fit to bootstrap
samples:

$$
\hat f_{\text{bag}}(x) =
\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat f^{*b}(x).
$$

For regression, predictions are averaged. For classification, trees vote
or average class probabilities.

## Random Forests

Random forests add a second layer of randomness. At each split, the tree
can consider only a random subset of predictors. This reduces
correlation among trees and often improves the average.

The main tuning parameters are the number of trees, the number of
predictors considered at each split (`mtry`), and tree size controls.

## Boosting

Boosting builds an additive model:

$$
\hat f(x) = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \lambda \hat f_b(x),
$$

where each new tree is fit to improve the current model. Important
tuning parameters include the number of trees, learning rate, tree
depth, and minimum observations per terminal node.

```r
library(caret)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)

rf_fit <- train(High ~ ., data = train, method = "rf", trControl = ctrl)
gbm_fit <- train(
  High ~ .,
  data = train,
  method = "gbm",
  trControl = ctrl,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

## Interpretation

Ensembles can be more accurate than a single tree but less transparent.
Use variable importance, partial dependence, and test-set performance to
explain what the model is doing.

## Worked Example

Compare a pruned tree, bagged trees, a random forest, and a boosted
tree model on the same prediction task. Use performance and variable
importance as discussion points.

## Applied Practice

Practice by comparing a single tree, bagged trees, a random forest, and
a boosted tree model on the same prediction task. Use resampling to
tune the models, evaluate them on held-out data, and decide whether the
gain in accuracy is worth the loss of transparency.
